title: Song Structure
intro: A song is a sequence of sections that repeat and contrast. The most common modern layout is verse–chorus with a bridge; the craft lies in making each section feel different while belonging to the same song.

items: Intro: sets key, tempo and mood, often with the chorus chords or the main riff.
Verse: tells the story; same music each time, new words. Usually lower in range and denser in words.
Pre-chorus: builds tension into the chorus, often ending on the dominant or a suspended chord.
Chorus: the main message and hook; same words and music each time, higher, simpler, more open.
Bridge (middle eight): a one-time contrast, new chords or key, before the last choruses.
Outro: repeats the hook, fades, or ends on a final cadence.

blocks.text: A typical layout: Intro – Verse – Pre – Chorus – Verse – Pre – Chorus – Bridge – Chorus – Chorus – Outro. Older forms still work: the 32-bar AABA song and the 12-bar blues (see Popular Forms (#/arts/music-theory/form/popular-forms)).
Listeners notice a new section when several things change together. Songwriters use:

items: Register: chorus melody higher than the verse.
Rhythm: short, wordy verse notes against longer chorus notes, or the reverse.
Harmony: a chorus that starts on I (or IV) after a verse on vi; a bridge that starts on a chord the song has barely used (often ii, iii or ♭VI, or IV if verse and chorus avoid it).
Harmonic rhythm: chords changing every bar in the verse, every two beats in the chorus (or the reverse).
Arrangement: fewer instruments in verses, more in choruses; drop out everything before the last chorus.

blocks.text: Prosody is the fit between words and music. Stressed syllables belong on strong beats and higher or longer notes; important words belong on the hook. Rhyme schemes shape sections too: a balanced scheme (AABB or ABAB over four lines) feels closed and suits a chorus, while an odd number of lines or an unrhymed final line (ABAC) pushes forward. Pattison's Writing Better Lyrics is the standard guide.

items: Take a verse you have written and write a chorus that differs in at least three ways: register, rhythm and starting chord.
Map the sections of a favourite song with timings; note what changes at each boundary.

blocks.title: Contrast
blocks.text: A verse uses vi–IV–I–V with busy, low melody notes. Suggest three ways to make the chorus contrast.
solution: For example: start the chorus on I or IV instead of vi; move the melody up by a fourth or more; use longer notes on the hook; change the chords twice as often (or half as often); add instruments or play the chords as fuller voicings.
blocks.answer: Change the starting chord, raise the register, lengthen the notes (and/or thicken the arrangement)

blocks.text: Sources: Pattison, P. (2009). Writing Better Lyrics, 2nd ed. Writer's Digest Books; Perricone, J. (2018). Great Songwriting Techniques. Oxford University Press; Webb, J. (1998). Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting. Hyperion; Covach, J. (2005). Form in rock music: a primer. In Engaging Music, ed. D. Stein. Oxford University Press.
